reference.source: ILAE classification and clinical guidance on the epilepsy syndromes
clinicalPearls: Genetic generalised epilepsy of early childhood characterised by myoclonic, atonic and combined myoclonic-atonic (drop) seizures.
Onset is usually between 1 and 5 years in a previously normal child, with a male predominance.
Drop attacks from myoclonic-atonic seizures cause frequent falls and injury.
EEG shows generalised spike-wave and polyspike-wave, often with a biparietal or central theta rhythm; the background may initially be normal.
Generalised tonic-clonic and absence seizures frequently coexist, and non-convulsive status epilepticus can occur.
Ketogenic dietary therapy is notably effective and is often introduced early.
Sodium-channel-blocking drugs and vigabatrin may aggravate seizures and are generally avoided.
Outcome ranges from seizure freedom with normal cognition to refractory epilepsy with intellectual impairment.
reference.pathophysiology: Doose syndrome is a genetically influenced generalised epilepsy in which thalamocortical network hyperexcitability produces bilaterally synchronous epileptic discharges. The basis is usually polygenic, with monogenic contributions in a minority, including SLC2A1 (GLUT1 deficiency), SCN1A and others; GLUT1 deficiency is important to identify because it responds to ketogenic therapy. The combination of positive (myoclonic) and negative (atonic) motor phenomena reflects rapidly generalising cortical discharges.
additionalInvestigations: Video-EEG capturing ictal drop attacks and interictal discharges
MRI brain, usually normal, to exclude a structural cause
Genetic testing including SLC2A1 and epilepsy gene panels
CSF-to-blood glucose ratio or SLC2A1 analysis for GLUT1 deficiency
Metabolic screening where the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Non-convulsive status epilepticus with fluctuating responsiveness
Seizure aggravation after starting an antiseizure medication
reference.prognosis: Highly variable; a substantial proportion achieve seizure freedom with preserved cognition, while others develop drug-resistant epilepsy and intellectual disability. Early effective treatment, including the ketogenic diet, may improve outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, which features tonic seizures, slow spike-wave and a worse prognosis.
Using sodium-channel blockers that may worsen seizures.
Missing GLUT1 deficiency, which is amenable to ketogenic therapy.
Overlooking non-convulsive status as a cause of apparent regression.
references: ILAE position papers on classification of the epilepsies
Panayiotopoulos CP. A Clinical Guide to Epileptic Syndromes and their Treatment
management: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medication such as sodium valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine or ethosuximide as first-line pharmacotherapy
Early introduction of ketogenic dietary therapy, which is notably effective and essential where GLUT1 deficiency is present
Avoid sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, which can aggravate myoclonic and atonic seizures
Identify GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1), as it responds specifically to ketogenic therapy
Injury prevention for drop attacks including protective headgear, with benzodiazepine rescue protocols for prolonged or non-convulsive status epilepticus
Neuropsychological assessment and educational support to address cognitive and developmental outcome
Genetic counselling given the genetic basis, with paediatric neurology follow-up
